title: Oct 15 Kussmaul–Rachmany call: each side identifies the other's weakness
description: On the Oct 15 call, the proponent of a single recognised certifier and the proponent of community-membership trust each named a real weakness of the other's option, and neither defended a central registry holding everyone's identity data. This is testimony that both bundled options are regarded as inadequate by informed advocates of each.
source: Call between Wes Kussmaul and Grace Rachmany on Oct 15, as described in the thesis text; recording or notes not independently consulted.

title: Historical failures and coercion of centralised certificate authorities and national ID gatekeepers
description: Documented cases in which a single trusted certifier was compromised (fraudulent certificates issued after a CA breach), coerced by a state, or used to deny service to individuals without appeal (e.g. deactivated national digital IDs cutting people off from benefits). These illustrate the single-point risk of option (1).
source: Public incident reports and journalism on certificate-authority breaches and national digital-ID lockouts; specific reports not consulted for this graph and should be attached.

title: Existing tiered assurance-level frameworks for identity proofing
description: Government and industry identity-assurance frameworks already define graded levels of identity-proofing thoroughness (e.g. remote self-asserted, remote with document check, in-person with document verification), and relying parties routinely specify a minimum level rather than a specific provider. This shows a public grading scale for check thoroughness is feasible and already used in practice.
source: Published identity-assurance-level guidance from national standards bodies and trust frameworks; specific documents not consulted for this graph and should be attached.

title: Market concentration in nominally plural trust ecosystems
description: In ecosystems designed to be plural — web certificate authorities, social-login identity providers, payment-card networks — a handful of providers end up carrying the overwhelming majority of relying-party trust, because relying parties default to whatever most users already hold. This is observational evidence that the thesis's failure condition is the default outcome absent countervailing design.
source: Market-share surveys of certificate authorities and third-party login providers; specific surveys not consulted for this graph and should be attached.
